newsitem.title: USA: $9 million drive started to win campaign reform.
newsitem.headline: $9 million drive started to win campaign reform.

text.p: A new election watchdog organisation Tuesday launched a well-heeled drive to ride the furore over campaign funding abuses into a drastic overhaul of the way federal and state races are financed.

Veteran election analyst Ellen Miller, head of newly organised Public Campaign, said $9 million had been received mostly from private foundations for a public relations drive to overcome congressional apathy and win passage of a system of financing campaigns with public money.

At a news conference, Miller conceded her effort was a longshot and "is not going to happen overnight." She estimated several years were needed to gain enough support for the plan to fund federal races with tax dollars.

A CBS News/New York Times Poll Tuesday showed the public favours campaign reform but 53 percent said President Clinton was more interested in keeping the present system and 68 percent believed the Republican-led Congress wanted to keep things the way they were.
But an overwhelming 78 percent opposed public financing of campaigns, saying it would cost too much.

The last campaign finance reforms came after the Watergate scandal over widespread campaign abuses and crimes that drove President Richard Nixon from office in 1974. But experts on all sides said those reforms, including limits on individual contributions and financial disclosure laws, are riddled with loopholes that permit unlimited "soft money" donations that indirectly help candidates.

The controversy over campaign tactics revolves mostly around soft money raised by Clinton's Democrats, including money solicited improperly from foreign sources as well as party officials luring donors with offers of coffees with Clinton and overnight stays at the White House.

Despite a daily drumbeat of funding abuse stories and federal and congressional investigations, Congress seemed in no rush to enact campaign reforms. Clinton has thrown his weight behind a bill with voluntary spending limits proposed in the Senate by Republican John McCain of Arizona and Democrat Russell Feingold of Wisconsin and in the House by a bipartisan coalition.

Even with Clinton urging passage by July 4, critics argue Congress is unliklely to pass major reforms since the present system of private contributions rewards incumbents over challengers. In 1996, 95 percent of incumbents won reelection.

At Tuesday's news conference, Miller's Public Campaign group refused to endorse the McCain-Feingold bill but promoted instead its own plan to give public money to candidates if they voluntarily agree to restrict spending. Miller estimated it would cost $500 million a year in public funding for congressional races if that system took effect.
The system backed by Public Campaign is based on a referendum approved last November in Maine that would give pubic financing to state candidates in 2000.

Acknowledging there would be little movement for sweeping campaign reform in Congress this year, Miller said her organisation would work on state reforms first. "So while our ultimate goal is reform of the federal system, we are going to first build support in the states," she said.
Money would be spent on advertising and a web site on the Internet to promote the grass roots effort, she added.
